newsitem.title: GERMANY: Berlin court pardons anti-Nazi resistance fighter.
newsitem.headline: Berlin court pardons anti-Nazi resistance fighter.

text.p: A German court said on Wednesday it had cleared the name of anti-Nazi resistance fighter Hans von Dohnanyi who was convicted of plotting to kill Adolf Hitler and executed during the last days of World War Two.
Dohnanyi's rehabilitation was the latest in a series of pardons granted to anti-Nazi resistance fighters who were convicted and sentenced to death by Nazi courts.
Prosecutors had applied to the court to quash the 55-year-old conviction after Dohnanyi's family campaigned to have his name cleared, Berlin justice authorities said.

Dohnanyi was arrested in 1943 and condemned to death for high treason in a tribunal run by the infamous SS, the Nazi party's own police and military arm that helped Hitler carry out his reign of terror in Europe.
He was hanged in Flossenburg concentration camp on April 6, 1945, four weeks before the end of the war when there was no doubt Nazi Germany faced defeat by the Allies.
It was "one of the worst cases of 'judicial' mistake made by the Nazis", the court said in a statement.

Germany's 16 federal states are responsible for lifting Nazi court verdicts where these were clearly unjust. But the procedure is a legal minefield which has left many of the most glaring cases still unsettled.
The need for action was highlighted most recently by the case of Dietrich Bonhoeffer, a Protestant clergyman executed at a concentration camp in 1945 for opposing Hitler.

Prosecutors applied in March last year for his high treason conviction to be quashed. After months of investigation, a Berlin court ruled it could not pardon Bonhoeffer as a Bavarian law had already exonerated him and his co-conspirators in 1946.
